title: Supplementary Data S1
text:
Preface
This document is the Supplementary Data S1 of the article GraphExperiment: infrastructure for high-dimensional quantitative data and associated networks in R/Bioconductor. It contains the use cases described in the article, with all code needed to reproduce them. Code and data are also available at https://github.com/almeidasilvaf/GraphExperiment_paper.
GraphExperiment (Almeida-Silva 2026) extends the SingleCellExperiment class with two new slots: rowGraphs, which stores graphs describing how features (e.g., genes, proteins, taxa) relate to each other, and colGraphs, which stores graphs describing how observations (e.g., samples, cells, cell types, species) relate to each other. Here, we demonstrate how GraphExperiment can be used with different omics data types through a series of short use cases, written in the style of package vignettes. All use cases use small example data sets distributed with other R/Bioconductor packages, and they can be run on a laptop.

1.1 Data description and processing
Here, we will use GraphExperiment to store gene-gene networks inferred from bulk RNA-seq data. We will use the maize (Zea mays) gene expression data set distributed with the BioNERO package (Almeida-Silva and Venancio 2021), which contains 28 samples from different tissues (Shin et al. 2020). From these data, we will infer a gene coexpression network (GCN) and a gene regulatory network (GRN), and store both in the rowGraphs slot of a GraphExperiment object.
The expression data are stored in a SummarizedExperiment object with a gene expression matrix (in TPM) and sample metadata. BioNERO also contains a data frame with maize transcription factors (TFs), which we will use to infer the GRN.

Next, we will infer a GCN with the WGCNA algorithm (Langfelder and Horvath 2008) as implemented in BioNERO. First, we need to pick the power \(\beta\) to which correlation coefficients will be raised to make the network fit a scale-free topology.

The object returned by exp2gcn() contains the adjacency matrix of the full network, which we will convert to an igraph object. Note that we will not filter edges here. The adjacency matrix represents a complete, weighted graph, with edge weights representing the (soft-thresholded) coexpression between gene pairs. Then, we will add module assignments and intramodular connectivities as node attributes.

# Convert adjacency matrix to an igraph object
gcn_graph <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
    gcn$adjacency_matrix, mode = "undirected", weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE
)

# Add module assignments and intramodular degree as node attributes
nodes <- V(gcn_graph)$name
modules <- setNames(gcn$genes_and_modules$Modules, gcn$genes_and_modules$Genes)
V(gcn_graph)$module <- modules[nodes]
V(gcn_graph)$kWithin <- gcn$kIN[nodes, "kWithin"]

# Identify hub genes and add them as node attributes
hubs <- get_hubs_gcn(exp, gcn)
V(gcn_graph)$is_hub <- nodes %in% hubs$Gene

1.3 Gene regulatory network inference
Now, we will infer a GRN using the ‘wisdom of the crowds’ approach implemented in exp2grn(), which combines the results of GENIE3, ARACNE, and CLR (Huynh-Thu et al. 2010; Margolin et al. 2006; Faith et al. 2007) and selects the top edges that make the network best fit a scale-free topology.

# Get TFs among the top 2,000 most variable genes
tfs <- intersect(zma.tfs$Gene, rownames(exp))
length(tfs)

[1] 31

# Infer GRN
grn_edges <- exp2grn(exp, regulators = tfs, nTrees = 1000)
head(grn_edges)

GRNs typically include only a subset of the genes, as genes that are not regulated by any TF (or that are not TFs) are not included in the edge list. However, GraphExperiment requires that nodes in row graphs match row names exactly. Thus, when creating the igraph object, we will include all genes as nodes, and genes that are not in the GRN will be represented as isolated nodes.

# Create a directed graph from the edge list, including all genes as nodes
grn_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(
    grn_edges, directed = TRUE, vertices = data.frame(name = rownames(exp))

section: 1.4 Storing networks in a GraphExperiment object
text:
1.4 Storing networks in a GraphExperiment object
Now that we have both networks, we can store them in a GraphExperiment object along with the expression data and sample metadata. We will also add gene-level metadata indicating whether each gene encodes a TF.

# Add gene-level metadata to `rowData`
rowData(exp)$is_TF <- rownames(exp) %in% zma.tfs$Gene
rowData(exp)$TF_family <- zma.tfs$Family[match(rownames(exp), zma.tfs$Gene)]

# Create a `GraphExperiment` object
ge <- GraphExperiment(
    assays = assays(exp),
    colData = colData(exp),
    rowData = rowData(exp),
    rowGraphs = list(gcn = gcn_graph, grn = grn_graph)
)

1.5 Exploring the networks
Since all data are stored in a single object, subsetting is straightforward. For example, let’s subset the object to keep only genes in the module with the largest number of TFs. Subsetting a GraphExperiment object subsets assays, rowData, and all graphs in rowGraphs simultaneously.

# Get the module with the largest number of TFs
tfs_per_module <- table(rowData(ge)$gcn__module[rowData(ge)$is_TF])
tfs_per_module

       14         9         2         2         1         3 

top_module <- names(which.max(tfs_per_module))

# Subset the object to keep only genes in this module

Finally, let’s visualize the coexpression and regulatory networks for genes in this module, highlighting TFs and hub genes. For visualization purposes, we will only display the strongest coexpression edges.

# Extract graphs from the subset object (with `rowData` as node attributes)
g_gcn <- rowGraph(ge_mod, "gcn")
g_grn <- rowGraph(ge_mod, "grn")

# Keep only top 5% edges in the GCN (for visualization only)
w <- E(g_gcn)$weight
g_gcn <- delete_edges(g_gcn, which(w < quantile(w, 0.95)))

# Remove isolated nodes from both graphs (for visualization only)
g_gcn <- delete_vertices(g_gcn, which(degree(g_gcn) == 0))
g_grn <- delete_vertices(g_grn, which(degree(g_grn) == 0))

# Plot GCN, with node size proportional to intramodular degree
p_gcn <- ggraph(g_gcn, layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_link(aes(alpha = weight), color = "grey60", show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_node_point(aes(size = kWithin, color = is_hub)) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey40", `TRUE` = "firebrick")) +
    theme_graph(base_family = "sans") +
    labs(
        title = paste0("Coexpression network (module '", top_module, "')"),
        color = "Hub gene", size = "Intramodular degree"
    )

# Plot GRN, highlighting TFs
p_grn <- ggraph(g_grn, layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_link(
        arrow = arrow(length = unit(1.5, "mm")), end_cap = circle(1.5, "mm"),
        color = "grey60"
    ) +
    geom_node_point(aes(color = is_TF, size = is_TF)) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey40", `TRUE` = "steelblue")) +
    scale_size_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 1.5, `TRUE` = 4)) +
    theme_graph(base_family = "sans") +
    labs(
        title = paste0("Regulatory network (module '", top_module, "')"),
        color = "TF", size = "TF"
    )

wrap_plots(p_gcn, p_grn, nrow = 1) +
    plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13))








Because module assignments, hub status, and TF annotation travel together with the graphs, any downstream analysis (e.g., finding TFs that are hubs in both networks) can be done with standard SummarizedExperiment syntax.

rowData(ge) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    rownames_to_column("gene") |>
    filter(is_TF, gcn__is_hub) |>
    mutate(grn_outdegree = degree(rowGraph(ge, "grn"), gene, mode = "out")) |>
    select(gene, TF_family, gcn__module, gcn__kWithin, grn_outdegree)

title: 2  Use case 2: protein co-abundance networks from single-cell proteomics
text:
2.1 Data description
Here, we will use GraphExperiment to store a protein co-abundance network inferred from mass spectrometry-based single-cell proteomics (SCP) data. Co-abundance networks are typically inferred with the WGCNA algorithm (Langfelder and Horvath 2008), which has been widely used in large-scale proteomics studies (Johnson et al. 2022; Seyfried et al. 2017), because soft-thresholding and topological overlap-based module detection are more robust than simple correlation thresholds.
We will use the data set from Khan et al. (2024), available in the scpdata package (Vanderaa and Gatto 2023b), which contains SCP data for 421 MCF-10A cells undergoing epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) triggered by TGF-\(\beta\), with cells collected at days 0, 3, and 9.
SCP data (as scRNA-seq data) are very sparse, which deflates correlations and makes co-abundance network inference unreliable. A common approach to handle sparsity is to aggregate similar cells into metacells before network inference (Morabito et al. 2023), which is what we will do here.
The data are stored in a QFeatures object (Gatto and Vanderaa 2025) with quantitative data at the PSM, peptide, and protein levels. Here, we will only use the protein-level data, without imputation of missing values.

About 80% of the values are missing, and nearly all missing values occur in proteins that are missing in all cells of a TMT set (i.e., an MS run). Thus, missingness is mostly determined by which peptides were selected for fragmentation and identified in each run, not by low abundances in individual cells (Vanderaa and Gatto 2023a). This has important implications for how we handle missing values. First, imputation methods that assume left-censored data (e.g., MinProb) are not suitable, as they would assign artificially low values to all cells of a set, creating spurious co-abundance among proteins that are missing in the same sets. This is aggravated by the fact that values are log-transformed relative abundances centered on each protein’s mean, so that low values do not indicate low absolute abundances. Second, the data must be corrected for batch effects (i.e., differences between TMT sets). Hence, following current recommendations for SCP data analysis (Vanderaa and Gatto 2023a, 2025), we will avoid imputation whenever possible, using methods that handle missing values directly.
Let’s add gene symbols to the rowData, since proteins are identified by UniProt accessions.
# Add gene symbols to `rowData`
acc <- sub("-.*", "", rownames(prot)) # remove isoform suffixes
rowData(prot)$symbol <- AnnotationDbi::mapIds(
    org.Hs.eg.db::org.Hs.eg.db, keys = acc, keytype = "UNIPROT",
    column = "SYMBOL", multiVals = "first"
)

2.2 Aggregating cells into metacells
To create metacells, we will first remove differences between TMT sets with limma::removeBatchEffect() (Ritchie et al. 2015), while preserving differences between time points. Since limma fits linear models to each protein using only observed values, missing values are kept as they are. Then, we will identify groups of similar cells with a principal component analysis (PCA) using the NIPALS algorithm (as implemented in the nipals package (Wright 2026)), which handles missing values without imputation (Vanderaa and Gatto 2025). To avoid restricting the analysis to the most consistently detected (and, hence, highly abundant) proteins, we will use all proteins detected in at least 30% of the cells.

# Remove differences between TMT sets, preserving differences between days
mat <- limma::removeBatchEffect(
    assay(prot), batch = prot$Set, design = model.matrix(~ prot$SampleType)
)

# PCA with NIPALS using proteins detected in at least 30% of the cells
na_prop <- rowMeans(is.na(mat))
sum(na_prop <= 0.7)

[1] 876

pca <- nipals::nipals(t(mat[na_prop <= 0.7, ]), ncomp = 10, scale = FALSE)
pcs <- pca$scores

# Proportion of variance in the top 3 PCs explained by days and TMT sets
sapply(c(day = "SampleType", set = "Set"), function(covariate) {
    sapply(1:3, function(k) summary(lm(pcs[, k] ~ prot[[covariate]]))$r.squared)
})

[1,] 0.77098150 0.043673608
[2,] 0.55986799 0.020346641
[3,] 0.03775828 0.002696338


The top principal components reflect differences between time points, not between TMT sets. Now, we will cluster cells from each time point with k-means, aiming at ~7 cells per metacell, and average the abundances of cells in each metacell (ignoring missing values).

# Cluster cells within each time point into metacells
cells_by_day <- split(colnames(prot), prot$SampleType)
metacell <- unlist(lapply(names(cells_by_day), function(day) {
    cells <- cells_by_day[[day]]
    km <- kmeans(pcs[cells, ], centers = round(length(cells) / 7), nstart = 10)
    setNames(paste0(day, "_mc", km$cluster), cells)
}))[colnames(prot)]

# Number of cells and TMT sets per metacell
summary(as.vector(table(metacell)))

  1.000   4.000   6.000   6.283   9.000  14.000 

# Average abundances in each metacell
mc_mat <- sapply(split(seq_along(metacell), metacell), function(i) {
    rowMeans(mat[, i, drop = FALSE], na.rm = TRUE)
})
mc_mat[is.nan(mc_mat)] <- NA
dim(mc_mat)

[1] 4096   60

mean(is.na(mc_mat))

[1] 0.5746053


Since metacells contain cells from different TMT sets, aggregation substantially reduced the proportion of missing values. Let’s see how this affects correlations between proteins (using only proteins with few missing values, so that correlations can be estimated for cells).

# Distribution of absolute correlations for proteins with few missing values
p <- na_prop <= 0.1
cor_cells <- cor(t(mat[p, ]), use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_mc <- cor(t(mc_mat[p, ]), use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

data.frame(
    level = rep(c("Cells", "Metacells"), each = sum(upper.tri(cor_cells))),
    abs_cor = abs(c(cor_cells[upper.tri(cor_cells)], cor_mc[upper.tri(cor_mc)]))
) |>
    group_by(level) |>
    summarise(mean = mean(abs_cor), median = median(abs_cor))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  level      mean median
  <chr>     <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Cells     0.164  0.131
2 Metacells 0.273  0.240


Absolute correlations increased substantially after aggregation, indicating that sparsity was masking co-abundance signals. For network inference, we will keep proteins detected in at least 80% of the metacells, as correlations estimated from few observations are unreliable. Since correlations in BioNERO are calculated from complete data, we will replace the remaining missing values (a small fraction) with protein means using BioNERO::replace_na(). Unlike left-censored imputation, mean imputation does not introduce artificial structure in the data, and it can only shrink correlations toward zero (i.e., it is conservative). Then, we will create a GraphExperiment object with metacells in columns, and store the mapping between cells and metacells in the metadata slot.

# Keep proteins detected in >=80% of the metacells and replace NAs
mc_mat <- mc_mat[rowMeans(is.na(mc_mat)) <= 0.2, ]
mean(is.na(mc_mat))

[1] 0.04530142

mc_mat <- BioNERO::replace_na(mc_mat, replaceby = "mean")

# Create metacell metadata
mc_md <- data.frame(
    row.names = colnames(mc_mat),
    day = sub("_mc.*", "", colnames(mc_mat)),
    n_cells = as.vector(table(metacell)[colnames(mc_mat)])
)

# Create `GraphExperiment` object
ge <- GraphExperiment(
    assays = list(abundance = mc_mat),
    rowData = rowData(prot)[rownames(mc_mat), ],
    colData = mc_md,
    metadata = list(metacells = data.frame(cell = colnames(prot), metacell))
)

Module assignments are now available in rowData, and time points are in colData. Thus, we can easily identify modules associated with EMT stages by correlating module eigengenes with time points.

# Correlate module eigengenes with time points

text:
3.1 Data description and processing
Here, we will use GraphExperiment to store microbial association networks inferred from 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing data, with taxon-taxon networks in rowGraphs and a sample-sample network in colGraphs. We will use the peerj13075 data set from the mia package, a core package of the miaverse ecosystem (Borman et al. 2025), which contains skin microbiota profiles of 58 genetically unrelated Indian individuals from three different cities and with different diets (vegetarian and mixed) (Potbhare et al. 2022).
Microbiome abundance data are compositional, i.e., sequencing only provides information on the relative abundances of taxa. Thus, standard correlation measures (e.g., Pearson’s or Spearman’s correlations) can lead to spurious associations (Friedman and Alm 2012; Gloor et al. 2017). To account for compositionality, we will use two widely used methods implemented in the SpiecEasi package: SPIEC-EASI (Kurtz et al. 2015), which infers a sparse graphical model (i.e., conditional dependencies between taxa) from centered log-ratio (CLR)-transformed data, and SparCC (Friedman and Alm 2012), which estimates correlations between the underlying (log-transformed) absolute abundances.
The data are stored in a TreeSummarizedExperiment object, the core data structure of the miaverse ecosystem (Huang et al. 2020). Taxa were already agglomerated at the genus level.

3.2 Inferring taxon-taxon association networks
Now, we will infer an association network with SPIEC-EASI using the Meinshausen-Bühlmann neighborhood selection method, with the sparsity parameter selected with the StARS approach (Liu et al. 2010). Note that spiec.easi() expects samples in rows and taxa in columns, and it performs CLR transformation internally.

# Infer network with SPIEC-EASI
counts <- t(assay(ge, "counts"))
se_mb <- spiec.easi(
    counts, method = "mb", lambda.min.ratio = 1e-3, nlambda = 30,
    pulsar.params = list(rep.num = 50, seed = 123)
)

# Get edge weights (symmetrized regression coefficients)
mb_weights <- as.matrix(symBeta(getOptBeta(se_mb), mode = "maxabs"))
dimnames(mb_weights) <- list(colnames(counts), colnames(counts))

# Create igraph object
g_spieceasi <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
    mb_weights, mode = "undirected", weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE
)
E(g_spieceasi)$sign <- ifelse(E(g_spieceasi)$weight > 0, "positive", "negative")

3.3 Inferring a sample-sample network
Microbiome data are often explored at the sample level, e.g., to identify groups of samples with similar community compositions. Here, we will create a k-nearest neighbor (kNN) graph of samples based on Aitchison distances (i.e., Euclidean distances of CLR-transformed data) with bluster (Lun 2025). For that, we will first perform a principal component analysis on the CLR-transformed data with scater (McCarthy et al. 2017), and then build the kNN graph from the top 10 principal components. Then, we will identify communities in this graph with the Louvain algorithm, and store community assignments as node attributes.

# Perform PCA on CLR-transformed data
ge <- runPCA(ge, assay.type = "clr", ncomponents = 10)

# Build kNN graph of samples
g_samples <- makeKNNGraph(reducedDim(ge, "PCA"), k = 5)
V(g_samples)$name <- colnames(ge)

# Identify communities of samples
V(g_samples)$community <- as.character(membership(cluster_louvain(g_samples)))

# Add graph to `colGraphs`
colGraph(ge, "aitchison_knn") <- g_samples

title: 4  Use case 4: cell-cell graphs for clustering single-cell data

4.1 Data description and processing
Graph-based clustering is the standard approach to identify cell populations in single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) data. In this approach, a graph of cells is built from a low-dimensional representation of the data (e.g., top principal components), with each cell connected to its nearest neighbors, and then communities are detected in the graph (Amezquita et al. 2019). Although cell-cell graphs are central to scRNA-seq data analysis, they are typically discarded after clustering, and there is no dedicated container for them in the SingleCellExperiment class. Here, we will use GraphExperiment to store cell-cell graphs in the colGraphs slot along with the expression data and dimensionality reduction results. We will use the mouse brain data set from Zeisel et al. (2015), which includes ~3,000 cells from the mouse cortex and hippocampus, available in the scRNAseq package (Risso and Cole 2025).
We will first load the data and perform standard processing steps, including quality control, normalization, selection of highly variable genes (HVGs), and principal component analysis (PCA), using scrapper (Lun and Kancherla 2023), which provides fast implementations of common single-cell analysis steps.

4.2 Building cell-cell graphs
Now, we will build a shared nearest neighbor (SNN) graph from the top principal components with scrapper::buildSnnGraph(), in which two cells are connected if they share any of their k nearest neighbors, with edge weights defined by the rank of the shared neighbors (Xu and Su 2015). This function returns a list with the number of vertices, the edges, and their weights, which we will convert to an igraph object with cell IDs as node names. For comparison, we will also build a kNN graph with bluster::makeKNNGraph().
Note that functions that perform graph-based clustering (e.g., scrapper::clusterGraph.se()) typically discard the graph or store it in the metadata slot, where it is not subset along with the cells. Using GraphExperiment, graphs are stored in a dedicated slot and kept in sync with the cells.

# Build SNN graph and convert it to an `igraph` object
pcs <- reducedDim(sce, "PCA")
snn_list <- buildSnnGraph(t(pcs), num.neighbors = 10, weight.scheme = "ranked")
snn <- make_undirected_graph(snn_list$edges, n = snn_list$vertices)
E(snn)$weight <- snn_list$weights
V(snn)$name <- colnames(sce)

# Build kNN graph
knn <- makeKNNGraph(pcs, k = 10)
V(knn)$name <- colnames(sce)

4.3 Graph-based clustering
We will now detect communities in each graph with the Louvain algorithm. Community assignments will be added as node attributes, so that they are automatically available in colData. # Detect communities in each graph and add as node attributes
colGraphs(ge) <- lapply(colGraphs(ge), function(graph) {
    V(graph)$cluster <- as.character(membership(cluster_louvain(graph)))
    V(graph)$strength <- strength(graph)
    graph

title: 5  Use case 5: cell-cell communication networks
text:
5.1 Data description and processing
Cell-cell communication (CCC) is commonly inferred from scRNA-seq data based on the expression of ligands in sender cell types and their receptors in receiver cell types. The result is naturally represented as a directed graph of cell types. Here, we will use GraphExperiment to store CCC networks in the colGraphs slot of an object containing pseudobulk expression profiles (i.e., with cell types in columns). This use case demonstrates that observation-level graphs can be stored at any resolution, including cells (see use case 4), cell types, samples, or species (see use cases 6 and 7).
We will infer CCC with LIANA (Dimitrov et al. 2022), a framework that runs multiple CCC inference methods and combines their results into a consensus ranking of ligand-receptor interactions. We chose LIANA because a systematic comparison of CCC methods showed that no single method consistently outperformed the others, and that the choice of method strongly affects predictions (Dimitrov et al. 2022), making a consensus approach a sensible default. Other tools, such as NicheNet (Browaeys et al. 2019), address a complementary question (i.e., which ligands best explain gene expression changes in receiver cells), and their output (ligand-target gene links) could be stored in rowGraphs. We will use scRNA-seq data of human pancreatic islets from Baron et al. (2016), available in the scRNAseq package (Risso and Cole 2025).

5.2 Inferring cell-cell communication

)))

6.1 Data description
In comparative genomics, data are often represented as matrices with features (e.g., gene families, orthogroups, synteny clusters) in rows and species in columns. Here, we will use GraphExperiment to store a matrix of phylogenomic profiles (i.e., copy number of synteny clusters across species) along with two graphs: a species-species graph derived from a phylogeny (in colGraphs), and a graph of synteny clusters with similar phylogenetic profiles (in rowGraphs). We will use data from the syntenet package (Almeida-Silva et al. 2022), which include synteny network clusters for 25 eudicot species from Zhao and Schranz (2019), and a microsynteny-based angiosperm phylogeny (Zhao et al. 2021).
We will also demonstrate how phylogenies (phylo objects) can be represented as igraph objects, since phylogenies are a special kind of graph (i.e., a directed acyclic graph, DAG).
The data set clusters is a data frame with genes and the synteny clusters they belong to, and the species tree angiosperm_phylogeny is a phylo object with 123 angiosperm species. We will first create a phylogenomic profiles matrix with the copy number of each synteny cluster across species.

6.2 Phylogenies as graphs
A phylogeny is a DAG in which edges point from ancestors to descendants. Thus, phylo objects can beconverted to igraph objects with the as.igraph() method from ape (Paradis and Schliep 2018). Here, we will first subset the tree to keep only our species of interest, and then convert it to a DAG with branch lengths as edge attributes.

# Subset tree and remove node labels (bootstrap support values)
tree <- ape::keep.tip(angiosperm_phylogeny, colnames(profiles))
tree$node.label <- NULL

# Convert `phylo` to `igraph`, adding branch lengths as edge attributes
dag <- ape::as.igraph.phylo(tree, directed = TRUE)
E(dag)$length <- tree$edge.length
V(dag)$is_tip <- V(dag)$name %in% tree$tip.label

Since the tree is now an igraph object, any graph algorithm can be used on it. For instance, we can obtain the matrix of shared evolutionary history between pairs of species (i.e., the distance from the root to their most recent common ancestor), which is the variance-covariance matrix under a Brownian motion model used by most phylogenetic comparative methods. For tips \(i\) and \(j\), the shared path length is \((d_{root,i} + d_{root,j} - d_{i,j}) / 2\), where \(d\) is the distance between nodes along branches.

# Get distances between all pairs of nodes
d <- distances(dag, mode = "all", weights = E(dag)$length)
root <- V(dag)[igraph::degree(dag, mode = "in") == 0]$name
tips <- V(dag)$name[V(dag)$is_tip]

# Get shared path lengths
shared <- outer(d[root, tips], d[root, tips], "+") / 2 - d[tips, tips] / 2

# Sanity check: same as the output of `ape::vcv()`
all.equal(shared, ape::vcv(tree)[tips, tips])

[1] TRUE


Nodes of graphs in colGraphs must match column names (here, species) exactly. Thus, DAGs representing phylogenies (which include internal nodes) cannot be stored in the colGraphs slot. Instead, we will store a species-species graph with edge weights representing shared evolutionary history (i.e., the off-diagonal elements of the matrix above), and a node attribute (root_distance) with the distances from the root to each species (i.e., the diagonal). Pairs of species whose most recent common ancestor is the root share no evolutionary history (weight of zero), so they are not connected.






Note



Native support for graphs containing nodes that are not observations (e.g., internal nodes of phylogenies and phylogenetic networks) is planned for future versions of GraphExperiment. For now, full DAGs can be stored in the metadata slot, as we will do below.



# Create species graph from the matrix of shared path lengths
phylo_graph <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
    shared, mode = "undirected", weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE
)
V(phylo_graph)$root_distance <- diag(shared)[V(phylo_graph)$name]

text:
6.3 Phylogenetic profile similarity graph
Synteny clusters (or gene families) with similar patterns of presence and absence across species (i.e., similar phylogenetic profiles) are likely functionally related, as genes in the same pathway or protein complex tend to be gained and lost together (Pellegrini et al. 1999). Here, we will create a graph of synteny clusters by connecting clusters with Jaccard similarities \(\geq\) 0.9 between their presence/absence profiles. Since clusters present in (nearly) all species or in very few species provide little information, we will only consider clusters that are absent in at least three species and present in at least three species. All other clusters will be included in the graph as isolated nodes, since nodes in row graphs must match row names exactly.

# Get presence/absence profiles of informative clusters
pa <- (profiles > 0) * 1
n_species <- ncol(pa)
informative <- rowSums(pa) >= 3 & rowSums(pa) <= n_species - 3
sum(informative)

[1] 1400

# Get Jaccard similarities between informative clusters
jaccard <- 1 - as.matrix(dist(pa[informative, ], method = "binary"))
jaccard[jaccard < 0.9] <- 0

# Create graph, including all clusters as nodes
profile_graph <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
    jaccard, mode = "undirected", weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE
) |>
    add_vertices(
        sum(!informative), name = rownames(pa)[!informative]
    )

6.5 Phylogenetic signal of synteny clusters
Finally, we will use the species graph in colGraphs to quantify the phylogenetic signal in the copy number of each synteny cluster, i.e., to what extent closely related species have similar copy numbers. For that, we will calculate Moran’s I (Gittleman and Kot 1990), using as weights the shared evolutionary history between species, which we can extract directly from the graph as a weighted adjacency matrix.

# Get weight matrix from the species graph
W <- as_adjacency_matrix(colGraph(ge, "phylo"), attr = "weight", sparse = FALSE)
W <- W[colnames(ge), colnames(ge)]

# Calculate Moran's I for each cluster with variable copy number
counts <- assay(ge, "counts")
variable <- apply(counts, 1, var) > 0
moran <- apply(counts[variable, ], 1, function(copies) {
    res <- ape::Moran.I(copies, W)
    c(I = res$observed, P = res$p.value)
})
moran <- as.data.frame(t(moran))
moran$padj <- p.adjust(moran$P, method = "BH")

# Add results to `rowData`
rowData(ge)$moran_I <- moran[rownames(ge), "I"]
rowData(ge)$moran_padj <- moran[rownames(ge), "padj"]

title: 7  Use case 7: comparative methods on phylogenetic networks
text:
7.1 Data description
Phylogenetic comparative methods (PCMs) typically assume that species relationships can be represented by a tree. However, reticulate evolutionary processes such as hybridization and introgression are common across the tree of life, and species relationships are often better described by phylogenetic networks, i.e., directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) in which some nodes (hybrid nodes) have more than one parent (Solís-Lemus and Ané 2016). Ignoring reticulation can bias estimates of evolutionary rates and lead to incorrect model selection (Morley et al. 2026), but PCMs that explicitly model trait evolution on networks are still scarce, with notable exceptions such as the extension of Brownian motion (BM) models and phylogenetic regression to networks by Bastide et al. (2018).
Here, we will demonstrate how GraphExperiment can be used as the core data structure for comparative analyses using graphs (instead of trees) to represent species relationships. We will use data on Xiphophorus fishes (swordtails and platyfishes) from Bastide et al. (2018), which include phylogenetic networks inferred with SNaQ and two traits (Cui et al. 2013): the sword index (length of the sword, an extension of the caudal fin in males, relative to body size) and female preference for a sword.
The helper functions used in this chapter (read_network_dag(), network_vcv(), vcv2graph(), graph2vcv(), and graph_gls()) are defined in the file code/phylo_graph_utils.R, and their source code is available in the Appendices.
The data comprise a file with three time-calibrated networks (with 0, 1, and 3 reticulations) in extended Newick format, and a CSV file with trait data.
# Read networks
networks <- readLines(here("data", "xiphophorus_networks_calibrated.tre"))

# Read traits
traits <- read_csv(here("data", "xiphophorus_morphology_Cui_etal_2013.csv"))

# Get major tree by removing minor hybrid edges

7.2 Storing species graphs in a GraphExperiment object
The trait data will be stored in a matrix with traits in rows and species in columns. One species (X. nezahualcoyotl) is not in the network, so we will remove it. We will also add a column with clade information (northern swordtails, southern swordtails, and platyfishes) to colData.

# Get trait matrix
tips <- V(dag_net)$name[V(dag_net)$is_tip]
trait_mat <- traits |>
    filter(tipnames %in% tips) |>
    column_to_rownames("tipnames") |>
    as.matrix() |>
    t()

trait_mat[, 1:5]

preference         NA       NA      -0.330       0.440         NA

# Create species metadata

    "Xbirchmanni", "Xcontinens", "Xcortezi", "Xmalinche", "Xmontezumae",
    "Xmultilineatus", "Xnigrensis", "Xpygmaeus"
)
southern <- c(
    "Xalvarezi", "Xclemenciae", "Xhellerii", "Xmayae", "Xmonticolus", "Xsignum"
)
species_md <- data.frame(
    row.names = colnames(trait_mat),
    clade = case_when(
        colnames(trait_mat) %in% northern ~ "Northern swordtails",
        colnames(trait_mat) %in% southern ~ "Southern swordtails",
        TRUE ~ "Platyfishes"
    )
)

Nodes of graphs in colGraphs must match column names (here, species) exactly. Since our DAGs contain internal nodes (ancestors) in addition to tips (extant species), they cannot be stored in the colGraphs slot as they are. Instead, we will store in colGraphs the species-species graphs that comparative methods actually use: the variance-covariance structure expected under BM. In these graphs, nodes are extant species, edge weights are the covariances between species (i.e., their shared evolutionary history), and a node attribute (variance) stores the variances (i.e., root-to-tip distances). These are computed with network_vcv(), which implements the recursive algorithm of Bastide et al. (2018) on the DAG: nodes are visited in topological order, and the trait of each hybrid node is the average of its parents’ traits weighted by inheritance probabilities.






Note



Native support for graphs containing nodes that are not observations (e.g., internal nodes of phylogenies and phylogenetic networks) is planned for future versions of GraphExperiment. For now, full DAGs can be stored in the metadata slot, as we will do below.

# Get variance-covariance matrices under BM

        tree_vcv = vcv2graph(vcv_tree[species, species]),
        network_vcv = vcv2graph(vcv_net[species, species])

7.3 Comparative analyses using graphs
Now, we will fit models of trait evolution using the species graphs stored in colGraphs. The function graph_gls() takes a GraphExperiment object, the name of a trait (row), and the name of a graph in colGraphs, and fits a phylogenetic generalized least squares (GLS) model under BM (or under a Pagel’s \(\lambda\) model, in which covariances are multiplied by \(\lambda\) to measure phylogenetic signal). Importantly, graph_gls() does not care whether the graph was derived from a tree, a network, or any other source (e.g., gene-sharing networks, ancestral recombination graphs, etc.); it only needs a species-species graph.

# Fit models for each combination of trait, graph, and model
fits <- expand_grid(
    trait = rownames(ge),
    graph = colGraphNames(ge),
    model = c("BM", "lambda")
) |>
    pmap(\(trait, graph, model) graph_gls(ge, trait, graph, model)) |>
    bind_rows()

Comparisons like this are straightforward when all candidate species graphs are stored in the same object. Finally, let’s store the best model for each trait in rowData, so that results stay synchronized with the data.

# Get best model for each trait and add to `rowData`
best <- fits |>
    group_by(trait) |>
    slice_min(AIC, n = 1) |>
    ungroup()

rowData(ge)$best_graph <- best$graph[match(rownames(ge), best$trait)]
rowData(ge)$best_model <- best$model[match(rownames(ge), best$trait)]
rowData(ge)$lambda <- best$lambda[match(rownames(ge), best$trait)]

In summary, by storing traits, species metadata, and species graphs in a single object, GraphExperiment provides a standard data structure for developing new comparative methods based on graphs. Developers only need to write functions that take a GraphExperiment object and the name of a graph in colGraphs as input, as we did with graph_gls(), and users can easily compare results obtained with different representations of species relationships (e.g., trees, networks, gene-sharing networks, or any other species graph).

Helper functions for phylogenetic networks
Here, you can find other pieces of code (Bash and R scripts) that were used in the main chapters. These pieces of code were stored in separate files to make the main text (i.e., book chapters) more readable.
Below is the source code of the helper functions used in Use case 7 to read phylogenetic networks as igraph DAGs, compute Brownian motion variance-covariance matrices on networks, convert them to and from species graphs, and fit phylogenetic GLS models using graphs stored in the colGraphs slot of a GraphExperiment object. These functions are stored in the file code/phylo_graph_utils.R.
#' Read a phylogenetic network in extended Newick format as an igraph DAG
#'
#' @param text Character with a network in extended Newick format,
#' with inheritance probabilities (gamma) after a double colon
#' (e.g., "#H1:0.5::0.3"), as written by SNaQ/PhyloNetworks.
#'
#' @return A directed `igraph` object (a DAG) with edge attributes
#' 'length' (branch length) and 'gamma' (inheritance probability), and
#' vertex attribute 'is_tip'.
#'
read_network_dag <- function(text) {

    if(grepl("#H", text)) {
        net <- ape::read.evonet(text = text)
    } else { # tree (no reticulations)
        net <- ape::read.tree(text = text)
        net$reticulation <- matrix(integer(0), ncol = 2)
    }
    ntip <- length(net$tip.label)
    node_names <- c(net$tip.label, paste0("node", seq_len(net$Nnode)))

    # Tree edges (including major hybrid edges)
    edges <- data.frame(
        from = node_names[net$edge[, 1]],
        to = node_names[net$edge[, 2]],
        length = net$edge.length,
        gamma = 1
    )

    # Get length and gamma of hybrid edges from the Newick string
    hyb <- regmatches(text, gregexpr("\\)?#H[0-9]+:[^,);]*", text))[[1]]
    hyb_df <- data.frame(
        label = sub(":.*", "", sub("^\\)", "", hyb)),
        defining = startsWith(hyb, ")"), # occurrence with a subtree
        length = as.numeric(sapply(strsplit(hyb, ":"), `[`, 2)),
        gamma = as.numeric(sapply(strsplit(hyb, "::"), `[`, 2))
    )

    # Update major hybrid edges (parent edge of each hybrid node)
    hnode_labels <- net$node.label[net$reticulation[, 2] - ntip]
    hnodes <- node_names[net$reticulation[, 2]]
    major_gamma <- vapply(hnode_labels, function(h) {
        hyb_df$gamma[hyb_df$label == h & hyb_df$defining]
    }, numeric(1))
    idx <- match(edges$to, hnodes)
    edges$gamma[!is.na(idx)] <- major_gamma[idx[!is.na(idx)]]

    # Add minor hybrid edges
    minor_edges <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(net$reticulation)), function(i) {
        minor <- hyb_df[hyb_df$label == hnode_labels[i] & !hyb_df$defining, ]
        data.frame(
            from = node_names[net$reticulation[i, 1]],
            to = node_names[net$reticulation[i, 2]],
            length = minor$length,
            gamma = minor$gamma
        )
    })
    edges <- rbind(edges, do.call(rbind, minor_edges))

    # Create DAG
    dag <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(
        edges, directed = TRUE,
        vertices = data.frame(
            name = node_names, is_tip = seq_along(node_names) <= ntip
        )
    )

    return(dag)
}


#' Compute the Brownian motion variance-covariance matrix on a phylogenetic DAG
#'
#' Implements the recursive algorithm of Bastide et al. (2018, Syst Biol):
#' nodes are visited in topological order (parents before children); for tree
#' nodes, covariances are inherited from the parent; for hybrid nodes,
#' the trait is a weighted average (weights = gamma) of the parents' traits.
#' Works for trees (DAGs without hybrid nodes) and networks.
#'
#' @param dag A directed `igraph` object as returned by `read_network_dag()`.
#'
#' @return A tips x tips variance-covariance matrix.
#'
network_vcv <- function(dag) {

    ord <- igraph::as_ids(igraph::topo_sort(dag, mode = "out"))
    n <- igraph::vcount(dag)
    nodes <- igraph::V(dag)$name
    vcv <- matrix(0, n, n, dimnames = list(nodes, nodes))

    # Update covariances of node `v` given those of previously visited nodes
    update_vcv <- function(vcv, i) {
        v <- ord[i]
        visited <- ord[seq_len(i - 1)]
        in_edges <- igraph::incident(dag, v, mode = "in")
        if(length(in_edges) == 0) return(vcv) # root

        parents <- igraph::tail_of(dag, in_edges)$name
        g <- in_edges$gamma
        l <- in_edges$length

        # Covariance with previously visited nodes
        vcv[v, visited] <- vcv[visited, v] <- colSums(
            g * vcv[parents, visited, drop = FALSE]
        )

        # Variance
        vcv[v, v] <- sum(g^2 * (diag(vcv)[parents] + l)) +
            sum(outer(g, g) * vcv[parents, parents] * (1 - diag(length(g))))

        return(vcv)
    }
    vcv <- Reduce(update_vcv, seq_along(ord), init = vcv)

    tips <- nodes[igraph::V(dag)$is_tip]
    return(vcv[tips, tips])
}


#' Convert a variance-covariance matrix to a weighted species graph
#'
#' @param vcv A species x species variance-covariance matrix.
#'
#' @return An undirected `igraph` object with edge weights representing
#' covariances (i.e., shared evolutionary history), and vertex attribute
#' 'variance' storing the diagonal of `vcv` (i.e., root-to-tip distances).
#'
vcv2graph <- function(vcv) {
    g <- igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
        vcv, mode = "undirected", weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE
    )
    igraph::V(g)$variance <- diag(vcv)[igraph::V(g)$name]
    return(g)
}


#' Extract a variance-covariance matrix from a species graph
#'
#' @param graph An undirected `igraph` object as returned by `vcv2graph()`.
#'
#' @return A species x species variance-covariance matrix.
#'
graph2vcv <- function(graph) {
    C <- as.matrix(igraph::as_adjacency_matrix(graph, attr = "weight"))
    diag(C) <- igraph::V(graph)$variance
    return(C)
}


#' Fit a phylogenetic GLS model (intercept only) using a species graph
#'
#' Models a trait as evolving under Brownian motion (BM), with the
#' covariance among species obtained from a `colGraph` of a
#' `GraphExperiment` object. Optionally, Pagel's lambda is estimated
#' by maximum likelihood.
#'
#' @param ge A `GraphExperiment` object with traits in rows and
#' species in columns.
#' @param trait Character, name of the trait (row) to model.
#' @param graph Character, name of the graph in `colGraphs` with the
#' covariance structure (as returned by `vcv2graph()`).
#' @param model Character, either "BM" or "lambda".
#' @param assay Character, name of the assay to use.
#'
#' @return A data frame with the estimated parameters, log-likelihood, and AIC.
#'
graph_gls <- function(ge, trait, graph, model = "BM", assay = 1) {

    vals <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(ge, assay)[trait, ]
    vals <- vals[!is.na(vals)]
    C <- graph2vcv(GraphExperiment::colGraph(ge, graph))[names(vals), names(vals)]
    n <- length(vals)
    dm <- matrix(1, n, 1) # design matrix (intercept only)

    # Profile log-likelihood for a given lambda
    loglik <- function(lambda) {
        Cl <- C * lambda
        diag(Cl) <- diag(C)
        Ci <- solve(Cl)
        beta <- solve(t(dm) %*% Ci %*% dm, t(dm) %*% Ci %*% vals)
        r <- vals - dm %*% beta
        sigma2 <- as.numeric(t(r) %*% Ci %*% r) / n
        ll <- -n / 2 * log(2 * pi * sigma2) -
            as.numeric(determinant(Cl)$modulus) / 2 - n / 2
        list(ll = ll, beta = as.numeric(beta), sigma2 = sigma2)
    }

    lambda <- 1
    if(model == "lambda") {
        lambda <- optimize(function(l) loglik(l)$ll, c(0, 1), maximum = TRUE)$maximum
    }
    fit <- loglik(lambda)
    k <- 2 + (model == "lambda") # number of parameters

    res <- data.frame(
        trait = trait, graph = graph, model = model, n = n,
        root_state = fit$beta, sigma2 = fit$sigma2, lambda = lambda,
        logLik = fit$ll, AIC = -2 * fit$ll + 2 * k
    )
    return(res)
}
